sentences.text: If you want to build a subway that costs four and a half billion dollars for just three stations, you don't build transit.
It's nineteen twenty-nine, and New York promises commuters a brand new subway line under Second Avenue to fix endless overcrowding.
Then the Great Depression hits, World War Two happens, and the project gets quietly buried for nearly a century.
When they finally restart digging in the two thousands, every single inch of dirt costs more than solid platinum.
Because underneath the street lies a hundred-year-old maze of mystery pipes, electrical cables, and forgotten steam lines.
Every time they move a single water pipe, it costs millions.
They're literally tunneling through a maze of financial regret.
Fast forward billions of dollars later: they finally open three shiny new stations, about two miles of track.
That means every single step you walk underground cost roughly a million dollars.
For that money, you could buy every daily rider a brand new car, and still have cash left for a private island.
So why did it cost so much?
Consultants, special contracts, and hiring six guys to watch one guy hold a shovel.
Phase two is still years from finished, which means the budget is about to enter orbit.
Congratulations, you've just built the most expensive hole in human history.
Send this to that friend who complains about his local train ticket price.
Hit follow for more engineering disasters.
